four-principles-of-design.title: Welcome to The four principles: contrast, repetition, alignment, proximity, part of Graphic Design.
four-principles-of-design.idea: Clients rarely describe what is wrong in design terms. They say it "does not pop", "looks cheap" or "feels busy". All three complaints are diagnosable: nothing dominates, so there is no hierarchy; nothing repeats, so nothing coheres; nothing aligns, so the eye cannot settle; and everything is equally spaced, so nothing reads as a group. Fixing those four things account for most of the perceived improvement between an amateur design and a competent one.
four-principles-of-design.example: A first card: the business name centred at 14 pt bold, the phone number at 12 pt, the email at 12 pt, the address at 11 pt, all centred, with four decorative shapes and a drop shadow. It is not terrible; it is vague. Nothing dominates, spacing is even, there is no alignment structure, and the decoration competes with the information. Four changes, in order: Contrast. The name becomes the clear first read at 20 pt in the brand colour; the role sits at 9 pt in letterspaced uppercase; contact details settle at 9 pt in near-black. The gap between levels is now large enough to see. Alignment. Everything moves to a single left edge at the same margin, with the logo on the far left and the details block aligned to it. Centred text is replaced by a strong vertical edge. Proximity. Name and role are 2 mm apart (they are one unit); the contact block sits 8 mm below (a different unit); the address is grouped with the contact details. Repetition. The three decorative shapes are deleted; only the logo mark, the brand colour and one typeface family remain — which is what makes the card recognisably from the same business as the flyer and the shopfront sign. Same content, same budget, same printer. The card now reads in the order the business wants: who, what they do, how to reach them.
four-principles-of-design.challenge: Design one complete set for a real small business — a flyer, a business card and three social posts. Use one grid, one type scale, one palette and one spacing scale across all five pieces, document your contrast ratios, and apply the squint and greyscale tests to each. Then revise: list every change you made after testing, and why the tested version is better than your first instinct.

typography-and-layout.title: Welcome to Typography and layout, part of Graphic Design.
typography-and-layout.idea: A beginner can be recognised instantly by their text: too many sizes, line height left at default, a paragraph as wide as the page, headings in a decorative script, and letter spacing applied at random. All of these are fixable with a handful of numbers and a little discipline, and the difference is visible before any colour or imagery is chosen.
typography-and-layout.example: A one-page A5 flyer for a training centre, assessed line by line. The original leaves line height at default, sets the body at 11 pt across a 130 mm measure, uses 14 pt for both the heading and the subheading, and puts a full paragraph of course details in centred text. The diagnosis, with numbers. The measure of 130 mm at 11 pt is roughly 100 characters per line — a third longer than the comfortable maximum, so nearly everybody skips lines. The heading and subheading differ by 2 pt, so there is no visible hierarchy. Centred text over six lines gives every line a different left edge, which is harder to scan than a single edge. Line height at default (1.15) is tight for body text, and the two-line paragraph touches the details block with no space between groups. The repair, with the same numbers made deliberate: body at 10.5 pt with line height 1.45 and a 75 mm measure in two columns; the heading at 28 pt and the subheading at 13 pt letterspaced (a 15 pt gap, unmistakable); left-aligned text on a 12 mm margin; 8 mm between the heading block and the body and 4 mm between paragraphs. The same content now takes 35 seconds to read instead of two minutes of struggle — which is the only metric that matters on a flyer.
typography-and-layout.challenge: Produce a small print pack for one real client or project — an A5 flyer, a business card and a poster — sharing one grid, one type scale and one palette. Document the numbers you used (sizes, leading, measure, margins, bleed), export print-ready files, and get them checked by a printer or somebody who has sent work to print. Record what the printer corrected, and update your own template with it.

colour-modes-and-file-formats.title: Welcome to Colour modes, resolution and file formats, part of Graphic Design.
colour-modes-and-file-formats.idea: A designer who has produced beautiful work on screen and sent a 72 dpi RGB JPEG to a printer for a 3-metre banner has learned an expensive lesson. The rules here are few, and they are the ones that turn a mock-up into a deliverable: choose the right colour mode, the right resolution for the viewing distance, and the right format for the destination.
colour-modes-and-file-formats.example: A client has a logo and needs it for everything from a shop sign to an app icon. The correct deliveries come from a single vector master, and each output has its own requirements. The vector master (SVG plus the working file) is the source of truth: scalable, editable, and the only file the client should ever need to send somebody else. From it: a print PDF in CMYK for a signwriter, rasterised PNGs at the sizes a website needs (with a transparent background), a favicon set (16, 32, 180, 192, 512 px), and social avatars at each platform's size. Two details that make the difference between a professional handover and a support problem. First, the small sizes need a simplified version: a logo with six details works at 300 mm and turns to mush at 32 px, so the icon set uses the mark alone, without the wordmark or the fine lines. Second, every colour is documented with its values — hex for screens, CMYK for print, and a Pantone reference if the brand uses one — with a note about the minimum size and the clear space around the mark. That document is a one-page brand sheet, and it is what stops the next person from stretching the logo or recolouring it.
colour-modes-and-file-formats.challenge: Prepare a complete delivery package for a real design job: a vector master, a print-ready PDF with bleed and embedded fonts, web and social exports at their exact dimensions, an app icon set with a simplified mark, and a one-page brand sheet. Have somebody else open every file — a printer or a developer if possible — and note every question they ask. Anything they had to ask about is something your package should have answered.

design-workflow-and-freelancing.title: Welcome to A design workflow, and getting paid for it, part of Graphic Design.
design-workflow-and-freelancing.idea: Most freelance design failures are not aesthetic. They are briefing failures (the client wanted something else, which nobody wrote down), revision failures (unlimited rounds, because nobody agreed a number), payment failures (no deposit, no written scope) and handover failures (the client cannot use the files, so every change costs another conversation). A simple process removes almost all of them, and it is what separates a designer who earns steadily from one who works constantly for less.
design-workflow-and-freelancing.example: A client asks for "a logo and a poster" for GH₵300. Accepting without a brief leads to eleven rounds of revisions, the client's nephew changing the design, and a request for the source files "just in case". The professional response is a quote based on estimated work, presented as a package with what is included and what is not. The estimate below prices 12 hours of work. Note the three things beginners omit: the discovery and brief (2 hours), the presentation and revision rounds (3 hours), and the export, handover and brand sheet (1.5 hours). Those are real work and are invisible in the final artwork. It also shows why the rate must include non-billable time. If a designer bills 25 hours a week — realistic with admin, marketing and quoting — then a GH₵60/hour billable rate yields GH₵1,500 per week of work, and the annual figure must also cover equipment, software, internet, data, electricity and the weeks with no work at all. A rate that ignores those is a rate that does not survive a slow month. Finally, note the terms: a 50% deposit, two revision rounds, final payment on delivery, and the licence explained in one sentence. The client sees a professional, and disputes mostly disappear before they start.
design-workflow-and-freelancing.challenge: Run one real design job through the full process: brief, deposit, three concepts presented in context, two revision rounds logged in writing, sign-off, print-ready and screen deliveries, a brand sheet, and a final invoice issued on delivery. Then write a half-page retrospective: where the work overran, what the client asked for that the brief had not covered, and the one clause you will add to your template next time.
